name: Jova
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Only comparative/bibliographical mentions exist (Shaul 2001; Valinas 1994; Pimentel 1865 2pp text); no descriptive phonology of Jova is documented.

sources.citation: Shaul, David L. 1983. The position of Opata and Eudeve in Uto-Aztecan. Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 8(2): 95-122. DOI 10.17161/kwpl.1808.480
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 'Vowels and Stress Patterns' (p. ~100-101, Table 2) describes stress for Opata, Eudeve, Tarahumara, Guarijío, Tubar and Cahita (second-syllable stress to the south; initial in Cahita; Op/Eu may have initial stress) but does not include Jova; Jova forms appear only in lexical sets (tevá 'earth', topa 'enemy', cachi 'sit', etc.) with acute = stress copied from the prayer's written accents.

sources.citation: Valiñas C., Leopoldo. 1994. El joba, como lengua sonorense, no es opatana. Anales de Antropología 31: 311-345. México: IIA-UNAM. DOI 10.22201/iia.24486221e.1994.0.23911
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress rule. Sec. 7 Fonología (pp. 329-331) gives a tentative consonant chart and says almost nothing can be said about vowels because of Spanish-based spelling; accent is mentioned only philologically: p. 323 notes the written accent on <tave-té> is notable because UA case suffixes are dominantly unstressed; p. 325 notes <oreirá> recurs 'sin acento gráfico' as <oreira>.

sources.citation: Sociedad Mexicana de Geografía y Estadística. 1888. Colección polidiómica mexicana que contiene la Oración dominical en sesenta y ocho idiomas y dialectos. México. ('Joba' text)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; primary text of the Jova Lord's Prayer with a few acute accents (motequán, mogitápejepa, tevá, cuguírra, veté, cá, oreirá, seeján).

sources.citation: Pimentel, Francisco. 1865. Cuadro descriptivo y comparativo de las lenguas indígenas de México, tomo II: 'El Joba', pp. 249-250. México: Andrade y Escalante.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; two pages giving ethnographic note and the Padre Nuestro text copied from the Sociedad de Geografía collection.

sources.note: The only other linguistic treatment of Jova by a Uto-Aztecanist; if anyone ventured a remark on Jova accent placement from the prayer's written accents (Opatan/Cahitan-style second-syllable stress), it would be here (Glottolog cites pp. 224 ff. for Jova).
